4. 
Whert Rulemaking Is Mandated or Necessitated by the Substantive 
Statute. Although Chenery II sets a default principle that agencies have 
discretion to implement their statutes through either case-by-case adjudication 
or rulemaking, it is always possible for Congress in the substantive statute to 
narrow or eliminate that discretion. Congress did not do so in the PUHCA, but 
in other statutes it has. The most obvious example is the common type of 
enabling legislation that requires the agency to conduct rulemakings on 
certain designated issues, often with statutory deadlines by which the rules 
must be promulgated, which are especially common in en vironm on tai 
regulation. Jacob E. Gersen & Anne Joseph O’Connell, Deadlines in 
Administrative Law, 156 U. Pa . L. Re v . 923, 939-40 (2008). A more subtle 
example is the type of enabling legislation that goes into practical effect only if 
the agency promulgates rules. A classic instance is section 361(a) of the Pubhc 
Health Service Act, 42 U.S.C. § 264, which in part provides:
The Surgeon General, with the approval of the Secretary is 
authorized to make and enforce such regulations as in his judgment 
are necessary to prevent the introduction, transmission, or spread of 
communicable diseases from foreign countries into the States or 
possessions, or form one State or possession into any other State or 
possession. * * * [T]he Surgeon General may provide for such 
inspection, fumigation, disinfection, sanitation, pest extermination, 
destruction of animals or articles found to be so infected or 
contaminated as to be sources of dangerous infection to Tinman 
beings, and other measures, as in his judgment may be necessary.
This grant of authority is wide in its breadth but, notably, it does not contain 
any restriction or prohibition that may immediately be enforced. Unless and 
until the Surgeon General (or other delegee) adopts regulations, the statute 
provides no basis for enforcement. For a recent high-profile application, see 
Alabama Association of Realtors v. Department of Health and Human Services, 
594 U.S. 758 (2021) (vacating stay of a judgment that the COVID-19 eviction 
moratorium rule, issued by the Centers for Disease Control, to which the 
Secretary of Health and Human Services had delegated the Surgeon General’s 
power, was beyond the authority granted by the provision).
